title: Oxygen delivery devices

BTS/ICS 2017 emergency oxygen guideline: only the December 2019 update-decision page read (target saturation ranges, reaffirmed after the 2018 IOTA meta-analysis); the full 2017 Thorax supplement itself is paywalled and was not read

objectives: Know the patient's ordered oxygen target range and titrate within the order.
Observe and record SpO2 and respiratory rate and escalate rising requirement early.
Keep oxygen equipment safe from ignition sources.

items.text: Oxygen is given to treat hypoxaemia within an ordered target range; AARC ranges are committee support (mostly level C), not graded strong recommendations.

The BTS/ICS emergency oxygen guideline uses two general target-saturation bands (UK practice): 94-98% for most acutely ill adults, and 88-92% for patients known to be at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (for example, some patients with COPD) pending a blood gas result. A 2018 meta-analysis raised a question about higher saturations and mortality, but the guideline's own update decision (reaffirmed, not a new recommendation) was that this did not call for a different target range.
Keep oxygen equipment away from ignition sources; for defibrillation follow the unit's oxygen-safety steps.
The decision to use the 88-92% scale should be made by a competent clinical decision-maker and recorded (RCP NEWS2; UK practice; other jurisdictions vary).
Know the ordered target range; if none is documented ask the prescriber. Titrate within the order or protocol and document each change with the reason.
Whether oxygen is a prescribed medicine and who sets targets is local policy; AARC does not say.
Device choice (cannula, mask, high-flow and others) and flow limits follow the unit's policy; this draft does not reproduce device flow tables.

Observe SpO2, respiratory rate and the patient's overall condition at the frequency set by the plan; increase frequency when the requirement rises. Check skin under masks, cannulae and straps (AARC 2024 recommends assessing skin around airway and NIV interfaces).
Staying with a patient whose oxygenation has fallen promotes safety and reduces fear.
Applying, changing and humidifying devices follows the unit's approved procedure.
SpO2, respiratory rate, work of breathing, device and connection checks each shift and after moves.

Monitor oxygen saturation continuously in sedated patients, and note respiratory rate, effort, lung sounds, secretions and whether suctioning is needed; after any intervention reassess heart rate, respiratory rate, saturation, lung sounds and the patient's own rating of breathlessness.
Escalate a rising requirement or falling saturation early rather than only turning the oxygen up.
Record device, flow, target range, SpO2 and each change with the reason per your unit's documentation standard.

checklist.text: Confirm the ordered oxygen target range; if none is documented, ask the prescriber.
Record SpO2, respiratory rate and overall condition.
Titrate only within the order or protocol and record the reason for each change.
Check device, connections and humidification each shift and after moves.
Check skin under masks, cannulae and straps.
Keep oxygen equipment away from ignition sources.

gaps: Device-specific flow and FiO2 tables: not reproduced; manufacturer sources needed.
High-flow and NIV device management: not covered; only the target-saturation band for hypercapnic-risk patients is sourced.

BTS oxygen guideline: only the December 2019 update-decision page was read; the full 2017 Thorax supplement (O'Driscoll et al.) is paywalled and was not read, so device-specific and dose-titration detail from it is not included.
